performers: Philadelphia Orchestra; Leopold Stokowski; Thaddeus Rich, solo violin
intro: In Saint-Saëns’s dance of skeletons, Danse macabre, Op. 40, a harp strikes midnight twelve times, and Death’s fiddle has its top string tuned down a semitone. Leopold Stokowski and the Philadelphia Orchestra recorded it in Camden, New Jersey, on 29 April 1925.

sections.label: A′ · Violin themes in full orchestra
sections.mNote: The full orchestra plays the solo violin’s themes.

sections.label: B · Dies irae in the woodwinds
A″ · Return of the dance themes
sections.mNote: The dance themes return, louder and more densely scored.

sections.label: Coda · Cockcrow and final solo violin

cues.title: Opening, harp strokes of midnight
cues.text: The harp plays a single note twelve times for the strokes of midnight. The note is D, the dominant of the G minor that follows.
cues.evidence: The Library of Congress’s NLS Music Notes (13 October 2022) describes the opening: a single note in the harp counting the twelve strokes of midnight. https://blogs.loc.gov/nls-music-notes/2022/10/song-stories-camille-saint-sans-and-danse-macabre/ Liszt’s piano transcription (Durand, 1921 edition, p. 1) opens on D. https://archive.org/details/31761037467115
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Solo violin, scordatura tritone
cues.text: The solo violin enters with its E string lowered to E♭. Its open A and E♭ strings sound together as a tritone, the interval older musicians nicknamed the devil in music. Saint-Saëns uses this tritone as the opening motif of the dance.
cues.evidence: The Palazzetto Bru Zane Mediabase entry for Danse macabre says the solo violin’s E string is lowered to E♭ to make the tritone used as the opening motif. https://www.bruzanemediabase.com/en/exploration/works/danse-macabre-camille-saint-saens IMSLP lists the violin’s scordatura as G, D, A, E♭. https://imslp.org/wiki/Danse_macabre,_Op.40_(Saint-Sa%C3%ABns,_Camille)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Durand, March 1876
cues.text: Édouard Colonne conducted the first performance at the Théâtre du Châtelet on 24 January 1875, and the reviews were mixed. By March 1876 Saint-Saëns could tell his publisher Durand that violinists no longer wanted their top strings tuned any other way than to E♭.
cues.evidence: The Palazzetto Bru Zane Mediabase gives the première at the Théâtre du Châtelet on 24 January 1875 with Colonne conducting, the “somewhat mitigated” reviews, and Saint-Saëns’s March 1876 remark to Auguste Durand. https://www.bruzanemediabase.com/en/exploration/works/danse-macabre-camille-saint-saens The Société Camille Saint-Saëns chronology records that the critics received the work coolly (“froidement accueillie”). https://camille-saint-saens.org/1875-1881/

cues.title: Dies irae in the woodwinds
cues.text: Around the midpoint, after a short fugal passage, the woodwinds quote the Dies irae, the chant of the Requiem Mass for the day of wrath. Saint-Saëns set it in a major key. Audiences of the time found the effect unsettling.
cues.evidence: The Library of Congress’s NLS Music Notes places the Dies irae quotation, played by the woodwinds, in the middle of the work. https://blogs.loc.gov/nls-music-notes/2022/10/song-stories-camille-saint-sans-and-danse-macabre/ William E. Runyan’s programme note puts it after a short fugal section. https://www.runyanprogramnotes.com/program_note/danse-macabre-op-40/ Andrew McIntyre (medici.tv, 31 October 2025) notes the major key and its effect on contemporary audiences. https://pageturner.medici.tv/en/the-spookiest-melody-of-them-all-dies-irae
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Xylophone in the orchestra
cues.text: Saint-Saëns added a xylophone to the orchestra, an instrument only recently admitted to the symphony orchestra; it imitates the rattling of the skeletons’ bones. In 1886 he quoted this dance in “Fossils”, a movement of The Carnival of the Animals.
cues.evidence: The Palazzetto Bru Zane Mediabase says the xylophone, only recently brought into the symphony orchestra, imitates the skeletons’ rattling bones, and that Saint-Saëns quotes the Danse macabre in the “Fossiles” movement of Le Carnaval des animaux (1886). https://www.bruzanemediabase.com/en/exploration/works/danse-macabre-camille-saint-saens

cues.title: Recording forces, Camden, 1925
cues.text: The Discography of American Historical Recordings lists the forces at the session: seven first violins, four second violins, three violas and two cellos. A tuba, a contrabassoon and a bass saxophone are among the winds, and there is a harp.
cues.evidence: Discography of American Historical Recordings, Victor matrices CVE-27929 and CVE-27930, Philadelphia Orchestra, Leopold Stokowski, Camden, New Jersey, 29 April 1925: instrumentation field lists 7 first violins, 4 second violins, 3 violas, 2 cellos, tuba, contrabassoon, 3 flutes, bass saxophone, 3 clarinets, 2 oboes, English horn, 2 bassoons, 4 horns, 3 trumpets, 3 trombones, timpani, accessory percussion and harp. https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/detail/800001918/CVE-27929-Danse_macabre_op._40

cues.title: Coda, oboe cockcrow
cues.text: In the coda a solo oboe plays the cock’s crow at dawn, and the skeletons scatter. The solo violin then plays a short elegy before the dancers return to their graves.
cues.evidence: William E. Runyan’s programme note describes the dance ending at dawn, heralded by a solo oboe depicting the cock’s crow, followed by the solo violin’s short elegy. https://www.runyanprogramnotes.com/program_note/danse-macabre-op-40/ The Library of Congress’s NLS Music Notes places the oboe’s crow in the coda. https://blogs.loc.gov/nls-music-notes/2022/10/song-stories-camille-saint-sans-and-danse-macabre/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Philadelphia Orchestra (orchestra), Leopold Stokowski (conductor), Thaddeus Rich (solo violin)
fields.note: The Discography of American Historical Recordings, from the disc labels, names the Philadelphia Orchestra and Stokowski. The solo violinist is credited only in the transferor’s description of the Internet Archive item, which names Thaddeus Rich; the labels as transcribed by DAHR do not.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Symphonic poem for orchestra with solo violin, 1874; the whole work on two disc sides joined into one file
fields.note: The transferor says the file joins the two sides of Victor 6505. The score edition and any cuts are not established from the sources.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Take date of the issued takes (take 2 of each side). DAHR also lists an earlier take 1 of each side under matrices C-27929 and C-27930.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Victor’s Camden studios; the DAHR entry names the city only.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: DAHR lists later issues of the same takes as Victor 6653/6654 and 01527/01528, and Gramophone (HMV) DB 961 and others.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: Twelve-inch double-sided Red Seal disc, Part 1 on one side and Part 2 on the other. Victor’s supplement of 1 December 1925 lists Danse Macabre by the Philadelphia Orchestra as 6505, 12-inch, $2.00.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: CVE-27929 (Part 1) and CVE-27930 (Part 2), take 2 of each
fields.note: Matrix numbers and takes come from DAHR. Take 3 of each was destroyed. No runout inscription has been inspected.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The Internet Archive item (added 16 September 2010) says “Transfer by Bob Varney from Victor 6505 issued in 1925”.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Archive’s date of addition is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: Equalisation, speed correction and noise reduction are not described. In this file the opening harp strokes sit close to concert pitch. A later Internet Archive transfer of the same sides (Philadelphia Symphony Orchestra – Danse Macabre, 2012, which is also the Wikimedia Commons file) runs about 2% faster and roughly a third of a semitone sharper, which is why this transfer is the one used.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public domain: Saint-Saëns died on 16 December 1921
fields.note: More than seventy years after the composer’s death; the underlying work is free of copyright in the EU and the US.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Public domain in the United States: first published in 1925 on Victor 6505; this transfer carries a CC BY 3.0 licence from its maker
fields.note: Victor’s catalogue supplement of 1 December 1925 already lists 6505 among the records issued since the last edition of its catalogue, so first publication falls in 1925 or earlier. US sound recordings published before 1 January 1926 are public domain under 17 U.S.C. § 1401 (Wikimedia Commons template PD-US-record-expired). Publication in 1925 also falls before the project’s 1963 cut-off for the EU phonogram term. The Internet Archive item’s licence field names CC BY 3.0, which applies to Bob Varney’s transfer.

composer.epithet: Pianist from the age of ten and organist for twenty years, known for the Organ Symphony, a dance of skeletons featuring xylophone, and a zoo suite he forbade anyone to publish.
facts: Piano with Stamaty; organ with François Benoist and composition under Halévy at the Paris Conservatoire, from 1848
Organist of La Madeleine, 1857–77; piano professor at the École Niedermeyer, 1861–65; co-founder of the Société nationale de musique, 1871
Symphonies, ten concertos, four symphonic poems, operas, organ music, songs and chamber music; also plays, poems and articles
Spent most winters from 1873 in Algeria, Egypt or the Canary Islands, and kept no fixed address from 1889 to 1905

quote.text: I have given it all that I had to give. What I have done I shall never do again.
quote.source: Saint-Saëns on the Organ Symphony, as quoted in Hugh Macdonald’s Boston Symphony Orchestra note

composer.background:
Camille Saint-Saëns was born at 3 rue du Jardinet in Paris on 9 October 1835. His father, a clerk in the Ministry of the Interior, died of consumption on 30 December, when the boy was not yet three months old. He was a sickly child and was raised by two widows, his mother Clémence and her aunt Charlotte Masson, who taught him piano. At two and a half he pressed the keys one at a time and waited for each note to die away before playing the next. By his own account he already listened at that age to the kettle on the drawing-room fire, which he called a “microscopic oboe”, and to its sound swelling until the water boiled.

Children’s pieces gave the left hand nothing to do. “The bass doesn’t sing,” he told his teachers in disgust, and was given Haydn and Mozart. On 6 May 1846, aged ten, he played Beethoven’s Third Piano Concerto and a Mozart concerto in B♭ at the Salle Pleyel, and played the whole programme from memory. Someone asked his mother what he would play when he was twenty. “He will play his own,” she said.
